papers.title: Inter-domain flexibility in F-Box proteins revealed by integrative modeling
papers.abstract: F-box proteins, the substrate-recognition modules of the SCF (Skp1-Cul1-F-box) ubiquitin ligase complex, play a central role in targeted protein degradation by enabling the selective recruitment of diverse substrates. F-box proteins share a common architecture with a conserved anchor domain linked to the substrate-binding domain. Despite extensive structural characterization of F-box proteins, their potential conformational dynamics remain poorly understood. Here, we employ an integrative modeling approach combining cryo-EM structures, cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS), and deep learning-based conformational ensemble prediction to profile the accessible conformations of F-box proteins. Our analyses reveal a significant inter-domain flexibility in FBXL2 and FBXL17 that enables sampling of a broad range of conformations within assembled SCF and CSN-SCF complexes. By contrast, other F-box proteins, including FBXL1 and FBXO22, exhibit intrinsic flexibility but are restricted to a considerably narrower conformational landscape. Together, our work highlights inter-domain plasticity as a tunable architectural feature of F-box proteins, which may shape their functional versatility within SCF complexes.

papers.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Translatomic Profiling Reveals Noncanonical RNA Junctions and Hidden Coding Potential in Porcine Epidemic Diarrhea Virus
papers.abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) poses a major threat to the global swine industry. Although coronavirus discontinuous transcription is well characterized, the classical model cannot fully explain the diversity of viral RNA junctions, while conventional genome annotations may underestimate viral protein-coding capacity. To address these gaps, we integrated time-resolved RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), cycloheximide (CHX)- and harringtonine (HAR)-treated ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq), comparative genomics, and peptide mass spectrometry to investigate PEDV RNA expression and hidden coding potential. RNA-seq revealed that, at 3 hours post-infection (hpi), the 3 genomic region exhibited strong relative coverage enrichment, whereas the relative contribution of the 5 replicase-coding region increased rapidly between 3 and 5 hpi, suggesting a possible transition from sgRNA-dominated RNA accumulation toward enhanced genomic RNA replication. Genome-wide junction analysis identified 43,635 distinct noncanonical RNA junctions, although canonical sgRNA junctions accounted for 95.5% of all junction-supporting reads. Several abundant noncanonical sgRNAs were predicted to generate novel coding products, including N-x4, N-x2, M-x3, and M-x2, short peptides encoded within the 3 untranslated region (UTR), and two distinct N-terminally truncated S proteins, thereby expanding the potential coding repertoire of PEDV. Genome-wide reading-frame analysis uncovered a pronounced asymmetry in hidden coding potential, identifying 68 overlapping open reading frames (ORFs) longer than 40 amino acids in the +1 reading frame, compared with only three in the +2 frame. Ribo-seq further revealed a progressive redistribution of viral ribosome occupancy toward structural protein-coding regions during the later stages of infection. By integrating HAR-associated translation initiation-site enrichment with CHX-based ORF-level translation analysis, we identified several noncanonical ORFs with strong translation-associated evidence, including N-x1, N-x2, S-x1, and ORF1b-x13. Moreover, peptide mass spectrometry detected a characteristic peptide corresponding to N-x1 in infected samples, providing independent proteomic evidence for the expression of this previously unannotated viral protein. Together, these findings uncover extensive noncanonical RNA synthesis and hidden protein-coding capacity in PEDV, establishing a foundation for understanding novel viral gene expression strategies and their potential evolutionary and pathogenic significance.

papers.title: Diverse bacteria exhibit superadditive growth on mixed classes of carbon sources
papers.abstract: Heterotrophic bacteria in nature encounter complex mixtures of functionally-distinct carbon sources, yet whether such diversity enhances growth yield across diverse taxa remains unknown. We grew dozens of strains from four phyla on defined mixtures representing five classes of carbon sources. Remarkably, many but not all strains exhibited superadditive growth on a dilute mixture of all 64 compounds--that is, yield exceeding the weighted sum of yields on more concentrated subsets of functionally-similar compounds. Using exometabolomics, pooled genetic screens, and proteomics, we find that superadditive growth is associated with enhanced carbon consumption in the mixed-class medium, combined with reduced dependence on amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis. Moreover, superadditive growth was predictable from genomes within the tested strain panel and correlated with genomically encoded sugar-over-acid preference. These findings reveal a previously underrecognized axis of physiological variation among heterotrophs and open the door to understanding the biochemical and evolutionary basis of this divergence.

papers.title: Both genetic and social inheritance influence female aggressive and submissive behavior in a wild primate
papers.abstract: Agonistic interactions are important determinants of resource access in wild animals, but their genetic basis remains poorly understood. Here we use a quantitative genetics approach to estimate the heritability of aggressive and submissive behavior of wild female baboons, considering relative rates of both individual and dyadic aggression and submission. To control for the social inheritance that creates kin-based dominance hierarchies, we implemented a multi-matrix model that included a social status similarity matrix alongside the additive genetic matrix. Despite a substantial contribution of social inheritance, especially for submissive behavior, we found heritable components for both aggressive and submissive behavior (h2=0.21 and h2=0.09-0.11, respectively). In dyadic models, aggressive behavior was primarily influenced by the aggressor's genotype (a direct genetic effect), while submissive behavior was primarily affected by the social partner's genotype (an indirect genetic effect). Finally, we found evidence for a negative genetic (but not phenotypic) correlation between aggressive and submissive behavior within dyads, and a negative genetic correlation between submissive behavior and eliciting submissive behavior. Together, our results highlight how direct genetic, indirect genetic, and social inheritance effects combine to influence primate social behavior.

papers.title: Parallel Trajectories in the Evolution of C-class MADS-box Genes in Flowering Plants and Conifers
papers.abstract: Gene duplication events frequently underpin phenotypic diversity due to the increase in genetic material that can be shaped by evolution. AGAMOUS (AG) genes are members of the MADS-box gene family that show conserved function in specifying reproductive organ identity in seed plants. While the function, expression, and evolution of these genes have been extensively studied in flowering plants, they remain understudied in gymnosperms. Consequently, little is known about how AG has contributed to reproductive diversity and evolution outside of the flowering plants. Here, we report that AG genes underwent two duplication events within conifers prior to the split between Cupressaceae and its sister family, Taxaceae. Further, we characterize the in situ expression pattern for each resulting paralog (AG1, AG2, and AG3) in seed cones of three Cupressaceae species, Metasequoia glyptostroboides, Taxodium distichum, and Juniperus virginiana. We discover gene expression patterns consistent with subfunctionalization: AG1 specialized in seed and sporangial development, AG2 in seed cone and seed coat development, and AG3 in ovuliferous scale development. This study provides an evolutionary mechanism for the development of unique seed cone reproductive traits in Cupressaceae. More broadly, our results uncover convergent patterns in the evolution of AG gene lineages across conifers and angiosperms.

papers.title: Circadian Clock Coordination of the Notch-to-Wnt Signaling Switch Promotes Regenerative Myogenesis
papers.abstract: Regenerative deficits of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) contribute to progressive muscle loss in muscular dystrophy. Successful regenerative repair requires a Notch to Wnt switch to allow MuSC expansion and myogenic differentiation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Leveraging complementary genetic and pharmacological approaches, here we identify the circadian clock as a key regulator of the Notch to Wnt signaling transition to promote regeneration with therapeutic potential for dystrophic disease. Circadian clock activity marks cycling myogenic progenitors during muscle regeneration, and clock induction occurs in concert with Notch activation. We identify that key components of the Notch pathway are direct transcriptional targets of the clock that were induced by clock activation. Mechanistically, clock coordination of Notch and Wnt signaling promoted MuSC proliferative expansion while facilitating myogenic progression during regeneration. Importantly, this clock-regulated mechanism was preserved in dystrophin-deficient mouse and human myoblasts, and clock-activating compounds enhanced regenerative myogenesis in dystrophic muscle. Collectively, our findings uncover a circadian clock-controlled mechanism that orchestrates regenerative signaling transition with potential for therapeutic targeting to restore regenerative capacity in dystrophic disease.

papers.title: RCDome: A Multi-Database Human Gene Atlas of Regulated Cell Death
papers.abstract: Introduction: Regulated cell death (RCD) governs tissue homeostasis, development, and disease, and is executed or regulated by specific genes. Yet for the researcher asking which genes execute or regulate a given RCD form, the answer is rarely simple: gene lists for the same form rarely agree across databases, many associations carry no traceable source, and most have never been systematically checked against primary literature. We built RCDome to answer the most basic question a researcher can ask: where did this gene-RCD association come from, and what is the evidence? Methods: RCDome is a multi-database human gene atlas built through a staged architecture integrating multi-source compilation, literature validation and evidence recovery, mechanistic classification, human-governed ontological adjudication, and web deployment. Five complementary evidence channels (PubMed Boolean search, curated databases, AI-assisted screening, manual curation, and Elicit systematic review) were integrated from 20 public databases into a unified matrix. Sixty-two original name strings were canonicalized into 53 RCD-related entities with curator-adjudicated operational definitions and ontological levels. Gene-RCD associations were systematically evaluated through an independent DeepSeek two-call LLM validation, Europe PMC full-text recovery and deep evidence extraction, an independent Consensus literature-search channel, and GPT-4o arbitration of disagreements. Source-grounding controls rejected extracted evidence not found verbatim in the source document, while the governance contract was enforced as executable code. Results: The compendium holds 22,473 association rows spanning 9,265 unique HGNC-validated genes (21,568 unique gene-RCD pairs). Evidence-first adjudication resolved 5,138 pairs (23.8%) as mechanistically involved; across the 4,775 role-resolved pairs, 225 (4.7%) are executors, 4,455 (93.3%) are regulators, and 95 are markers, revealing a small death-executing core embedded in a vast regulatory network. Under a separate seven-class mechanistic criterion applied to all 22,473 rows, only 3,063 (13.6%) were mechanistically confirmed and 286 (1.3%) were database-only with no verifiable paper trail. Conclusion: RCDome makes the RCD evidence landscape measurable and traceable, showing that AI-assisted curation can be verifiable, human-governed, and explicit about uncertainty. It is delivered as a Shiny web application that lets any researcher query the atlas and inspect the evidence behind each association. Availability: RCDome is freely available at https://rcdome.org/ (source code and data at https://github.com/BioCancerInformatics/RCDome).

papers.title: Thienothiazolocarboxamides: rapidly cidal agents causing catastrophic thiol collapse in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
papers.abstract: Thienothiazolocarboxamides (TTCs) were discovered as a hit in a whole cell screen for new antituberculosis agents. These molecules were rapidly cidal under both replicating and non-replicating conditions and killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in macrophages. The heterobicyclic core of this scaffold was essential for activity and resistance to these agents was mediated by loss of EthA, a flavin containing monooxygenase also responsible for the bioactivation of ethionamide. EthA-mediated activation of TTCs in whole cells was found to produce mycothiol adducts and RNAseq profiles revealed a mechanism of action identical to the fungal mycotoxins patulin and nidulalin A. EthA oxidizes the sulfur of the thiazole ring to create a relatively stable sulfenic acid that reacts with cellular thiols. This unique, replication-independent, mechanism suggests the possibility that these molecules may contribute significantly to shortening the duration of tuberculosis chemotherapy.

papers.title: Low-fidelity simulator selection for multi-fidelity inference of epithelial vertex models
papers.abstract: Vertex models link cell division, neighbour exchange, and intercellular forces to epithelial tissue form through parameters such as junctional line tension and perimeter contractility. Bayesian inference of these parameters from data quantifies their uncertainty, but for stochastic models of proliferating tissues it requires many costly simulations. Multi-fidelity simulation-based inference reduces this cost by training on many runs of a cheaper, less accurate ('low-fidelity') simulator before refining with a few full ('high-fidelity') runs. Low-fidelity versions can be constructed in several ways, for example by stopping simulations early, coarsening the timestep, or averaging fewer replicates, but it is unclear which to choose before committing to costly training. To address this, we introduce PRISM (Paired Ranking Index for Simulator Matching), a screen that compares each candidate with the full simulator on paired runs, scoring agreement in cell-packing statistics against cost. For a vertex model of a proliferating tissue, PRISM flags stopping early as unreliable before training; once trained, this choice can produce confidently wrong parameter estimates. By contrast, a coarser timestep, within the range tested, is cheap and accurate; while fewer replicates are accurate but too costly. Using a screened low-fidelity simulator, multi-fidelity inference outperforms approximate Bayesian computation and neural-network inference trained on full simulations alone, at matched cost and with well-calibrated uncertainty. The same pattern recurs for a second vertex model fitted to published Drosophila pupal-wing imaging data, although there stopping halfway proves safe. Together, our findings suggest that which approximations are safe depends on the model, and that screening them before training makes multi-fidelity inference of tissue mechanics practical.

papers.title: Calibrating developmental dynamics from single-cell atlases: lineage paths outrun least-action routes
papers.abstract: Single-cell atlases infer developmental dynamics from destructive snapshots, yet how far realized lineage paths depart from such inferred dynamics has never been measured with controls. We introduce LADD (Least-Action Developmental Dynamics), a measurement framework that learns a stochastic developmental vector field from time-series single-cell RNA-seq and computes minimum-action and minimum-time paths, together with a three-layer calibration protocol that separates genuine path deviation from the generic cost of centroid measurement, and we compare its forecasting component with optimal-transport and flow-matching methods. In the lineage-resolved Caenorhabditis elegans atlas, the raw action ratio of observed lineage-centroid trajectories to optimal paths is 3.79, yet forward-simulated ensembles of the learned model itself score 2.07, leaving a genuine excess of about two-fold. In zebrafish (Danio rerio), the observed ratio sits entirely at the model's floor. Three mechanisms that could explain the residual deviation (detours, flow-opposition, and fate-map complexity) are each excluded; what remains is speed, with lineages moving 30-43% faster along the learned flow. We report validity boundaries for temporal resolution, cross-species comparison, and energetic interpretation, delimiting where action-based trajectory comparisons are meaningful.

papers.title: Choice of annotation data significantly impacts automated reconstruction of genome-scale metabolic networks
papers.abstract: Genome-scale metabolic models are valuable tools for studying metabolism in many applications, such as metabolic engineering or understanding human disease. However, curated models are available for only a limited number of organisms, and generating high-quality models for additional organisms remains a challenge. To help address this challenge, several software tools have been developed that can produce draft models in an automated fashion, but the quality of these draft models lags behind manually curated ones. Thus, there is still a need to improve these tools. Previous work has focused primarily on developing better methods for each step in the reconstruction process, such as gene annotation and gap-filling. Here, we focus on the data that underlies these methods, such as known connections between protein sequence and function. We find that changing the source of reconstruction data has a substantial impact on the contents and predictions of generated models. In fact, the source of data can have a bigger impact than the choice of reconstruction method. Additionally, we show that the reconstruction process is sensitive to the accuracy of gene annotations in the reconstruction data. Finally, we demonstrate the importance of having functional annotation data from an organism that is closely related to the one for which a model is being built. These observations highlight the importance of reconstruction data and identify principles that should be considered when selecting data for reconstruction tools.

papers.title: Glycolysis and interferon transcription in melanoma immunotherapy
papers.abstract: Glycolysis and interferon signalling have both been associated with responses to PD-1 blockade, but their joint transcriptional relationship with treatment outcome remains uncertain. We examined whether a state with high glycolysis and low interferon- response was associated with reduced disease control in melanoma. Fixed Hallmark gene sets were scored by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis in GSE91061, GSE78220 and an additional Liu cohort. Disease control analyses included 47, 26 and 100 patients. Conditional odds ratios for the joint state were 6.06 (exact 95% confidence interval, 1.04 to 65.61), 0.35 (0.026 to 3.11) and 1.03 (0.39 to 2.73), respectively. Holm-adjusted P values for the two initial comparisons were 0.073 and 0.365. The additional exploratory P value was 1.000. Continuous models and analyses that omitted each patient in turn did not provide consistent evidence of an adverse association. IFN scores were negatively correlated with DNA-derived tumour purity in 102 patients (Spearman {rho} = -0.671). Among 40 patients with paired biopsies, disease control was associated with higher on-treatment IFN scores after baseline adjustment, although the paired subset had lower baseline glycolysis than patients without paired profiles. In patient-level single-cell analyses, the baseline CD8 T cell correlation weakened when an alternative rank score used a common gene background. The defined joint state was not consistently associated with poorer disease control across cohorts. Bulk IFN scores were related to tumour purity, and cellular correlations were sensitive to scoring choices. These transcriptomic results do not measure pyruvate concentration, glycolytic flux or STAT1 pyruvylation.

papers.title: Tfcp2l1 recruits Thrap3 to sustain ESC self-renewal via Jmjd1c exon-5 splicing and DNA repair choice
papers.abstract: How embryonic stem cells (ESCs) maintain genomic integrity while sustaining self-renewal remains poorly understood. We find that transcription factor CP2-like 1 (Tfcp2l1) recruits Thrap3 in mouse ESCs, where this complex maintains RNA polymerase II activity and promotes transcription of Tfcp2l1 target genes. In addition, Thrap3 supports mESC self-renewal. Interestingly, knockdown of either Tfcp2l1 or Thrap3 induces highly overlapping alternative-splicing changes, including reduced inclusion of exon-5 in Jmjd1c. Further studies reveal that skipping of Jmjd1c exon-5 weakens the association between Jmjd1c and Mdc1, accompanied by elevated Mdc1-associated dimethylation, leading to reduced Mdc1 and Rnf8 interaction and diminished K63-linked ubiquitin signalling. These alterations impair chromatin recruitment of the Rap80 and Brca1 repair complex and increase Rad51 foci formation, indicative of a shift in DNA repair pathway preference. Accordingly, loss of Tfcp2l1 or Thrap3 results in accumulated DNA damage, hypersensitivity to genotoxic stress, compromised ESC self-renewal and enhanced apoptosis. Similar phenotypes can be recapitulated in human ESCs. Together, our findings provide new insights into how ESCs coordinate genome maintenance with self-renewal.

papers.title: The role of Plasmodium falciparum acyl-coenzyme A synthetase 10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis
papers.abstract: During the asexual blood stage, malaria parasites synthesize large quantities of lipids to support their rapid proliferation. Exogenous fatty acids obtained from host plasma are activated for lipid synthesis by parasite acyl-coenzyme A synthetases (ACSs). Of the twelve Plasmodium falciparum ACS homologs, ACS10 has emerged as a key blood-stage enzyme. Here, we sought to define the role of ACS10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis during asexual development. To accomplish this, we have employed fatty acid alkyne probes of parasite lipid synthesis together with selective depletion of ACS10 in a conditional knockdown parasite line. This approach revealed that ACS10 is required for efficient incorporation of 16- to 20-carbon unsaturated fatty acid alkynes and a 20-carbon, saturated fatty acid alkyne into the major parasite phospholipids and neutral lipids. In contrast, shorter saturated fatty acid alkynes were either unaffected by ACS10 depletion or were hyper-incorporated into parasite lipids. ACS10 knockdown elicited a profound deformation of the food vacuole, which was likely caused by an imbalance of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids in parasite lipids. To promote the discovery and characterization of ACS inhibitors, we have established a fatty acid alkyne-based approach for identifying compounds that target ACS10 as their primary mode of action.

papers.title: SPARK: Systematic Profiling of Antibiotic-Phage Response Kinetics
papers.abstract: Phage therapy is, in practice, combination therapy: phage are almost always added to an ongoing antibiotic regimen, yet the combination is rarely designed to have a specific interaction pattern. Interactions can be antagonistic, additive or synergistic and cannot be inferred from either agent alone. Here we introduce SPARK, a method which quantifies phage antibiotic interaction from growth curves as the integrated deviation of observed growth from the growth expected under Bliss independence. We profiled 42 combinations spanning the ESKAPE pathogens and Escherichia coli with twelve antibiotics. We show that i) synergy and antagonism are resolvable within a single high-throughput assay, with the interaction determined by the phage antibiotic bacteria pairing; ii) 21 clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates differ among themselves as widely as the seven species do; and, iii) interactions change between a few hours and two days, several reversing direction. Overall, SPARK needs only a plate reader and the analysis is performed with a specific openly available web tool.

papers.title: MmuPV1 and HPV E6 Elevate Nuclear Accumulation of IKK? to Impair NF-κB Signaling to Promote Persistent Infection
papers.abstract: The mouse papillomavirus (MmuPV1) E6 oncoprotein is essential for persistent infection and cancer development. Previous studies identified amino acid R130 of MmuPV1 E6 as critical for its interaction with the tumor suppressor MAML1. Mutation of this residue (R130A) disrupts MAML1 binding and prevents disease development in mice. In this study, we demonstrate that MmuPV1 E6 also disrupts NF-{kappa}B signaling through interactions with proteins in the I{kappa}B kinase (IKK) complex. Specifically, the MmuPV1 E6R130A mutant is defective in binding IKK complex proteins and fails to impair NF-{kappa}B signaling in mouse keratinocytes, suggesting that these interactions are necessary for E6-mediated disruption of this pathway. Furthermore, MmuPV1 E6 expression is associated with increased nuclear localization of IKK?, whereas cells expressing the E6R130A mutant exhibit no such increase. These findings suggest that E6-mediated nuclear localization of IKK? depends on its interaction with IKK complex proteins. Importantly, we demonstrate that the human papillomavirus HPV16 E6 oncoprotein similarly impairs NF-{kappa}B signaling and increases nuclear IKK? localization in human keratinocytes, suggesting a shared mechanism between mouse and human papillomaviruses. Additionally, analysis of previously published RNA sequencing data reveals that MmuPV1 E6 induces several transcriptional changes associated with increased nuclear IKK?. Together, these findings demonstrate that both MmuPV1 and HPV16 E6 disrupt NF-{kappa}B signaling in association with increased nuclear IKK? localization. This study provides the first evidence of an E6 oncoprotein interacting with and changing subcellular localization of IKK? to disrupt cellular homeostasis.

papers.title: Seasonal H1N1 influenza A virus preferentially infects a pre-existing ciliogenesis-primed secretory cell state
papers.abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAV) infect secretory and ciliated cells of the human airway epithelium , but whether all cells within one cell type are equally susceptible to infection remains unresolved. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of primary human bronchial epithelial cultures from three donors identified preferential infection of a transcriptionally distinct subpopulation of secretory cells by seasonal H1N1 IAV A/Hawaii/70/2019 . Genes upregulated in this subpopulation showed enrichment for cilium-related gene ontology terms. In an ex post facto approach, this enrichment persisted after excluding genes differentially expressed between infected and mock-treated samples, including those identified in secretory cell-specific comparisons. Single-cell analysis further revealed no significant increase in ciliogenesis scores in infected secretory cells compared to mock infected cells at 6 hours post-infection , arguing against infection-induced activation of the canonical ciliogenesis programme during the initial viral replication cycle . Collectively, these results support preferential infection of ciliogenesis-primed secretory cells and refine IAV tropism beyond cell type to encompass epithelial differentiation state.

papers.title: Structural and functional examination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae TfpC reveals a dynamic two-domain architecture required for type IV pilus function
papers.abstract: The Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gc) Type IV pilus (T4p) is a critical apparatus for colonization and virulence. This molecular machine resides at the host-pathogen interface and mediates adherence to host cells, twitching motility, natural transformation, and resistance to oxidative agents. Previously, we identified a DUF4124 family, T4p component, TfpC. TfpC is required for full T4p elaboration, and deleting the tfpC gene reduced natural transformation competence and resulted in an under-piliated colony morphology. Our earlier models suggested TfpC is composed of an N-terminal transmembrane helix and a proline-rich disordered region followed by a C-terminal coiled-coil. Here, we used targeted structural and genetic approaches to define TfpC's molecular structure. Our new data show that TfpC's N-terminal domain forms a novel, dynamic three-stranded {beta}-sheet structure. These data indicate that the flexible disordered region acts as a linker between the N- and C-terminal domains. Functionally, we illustrate TfpC requires an acidic face within the C-terminal coiled-coil domain to mediate pilus biogenesis and function. This study characterizes a unique protein fold and family and defines the contributions of TfpC's domains to its function.

papers.title: Polyphosphate metabolism genes are associated with hydroxyapatite biomineralization capacity in a novel hydrogenotrophic methanogen Methanobacterium AMB_03
papers.abstract: Methanogenic archaea play crucial roles in sedimentary phosphorus cycling, but their capacity for phosphate biomineralization remains poorly understood. Here we demonstrate that Methanobacterium AMB_03, isolated from a serpentinizing environment, mediates extracellular precipitation of carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite (HAp) under phosphate-enriched conditions. Comparative genomic analysis of AMB_03 versus non-mineralizing strains (Methanobacterium oryzae, Methanoculleus bourgensis MAB1) shows that AMB_03 encodes polyphosphate kinase 1 (ppk1), enabling polyphosphate synthesis from ATP. In contrast, M. oryzae and MAB1 completely lack ppk1, preventing polyphosphate accumulation. Phylogenomic analysis of 320 Methanobacteriota genomes further shows that complete polyP cycling capacity is present in only ~25% of representatives, placing AMB_03 among a minority of methanogens with this capability. Experimental cultivation across phosphate gradients (0-6 mM) showed HAp early-onset precipitation was preferential at [≥]3 mM. Precipitation was eventually observed at all phosphate concentrations (except P0) by 49 weeks and was associated with extracellular polymeric substance production and localized pH increases of up to 8.08. Raman spectroscopy confirmed carbonate-substituted HAp, with characteristic peaks at 960.5 cm-1 (PO43-) and 1070-1072 cm-1 (CO32-). These findings identify a strong genomic association between polyphosphate metabolism genes and biomineralization capacity, suggesting that methanogens with complete polyP cycling systems may create localized phosphate-rich environments that promote authigenic mineral formation in sedimentary systems.

papers.title: Environmental Frass Remodels the Larval Gut Microbiome to Enable Black Soldier Fly (Hermetia illucens) Bioconversion of Livestock Manure
papers.abstract: Black Soldier Fly larvae (BSFL) consume nearly any organic material and show promise for the remediation of agricultural waste, including livestock manure. BSFL feeding generates frass, a mixture of unconsumed substrate, larval feces, and microorganisms. We identified a wild population of BSFL (Yuba strain) thriving on rabbit manure, a challenging substrate due to its high lignocellulose content. We investigated if frass extract from this source was necessary and sufficient to support bioconversion of manure and if such effects are altered by captive husbandry. Larvae supplemented with domestic frass failed to grow on rabbit manure but grew well when supplemented with wild-sourced frass. Microbiome analysis revealed that wild-sourced frass contributes a cohort of lignocellulose-degrading microorganisms to the BSFL gut, particularly Rummeliibacillus bacteria and Scedosporium fungi. These growth-promoting effects extended to cattle manure. Following initial seeding with wild-sourced frass, lab-cultured frass ultimately failed to support growth on rabbit manure and the gut microbiome shifted toward bacteria commonly found in domestic BSFL. This study reveals that frass extract derived from environmental sources can improve the bioconversion ability of BSFL and that beneficial microbes are lost during captive-rearing.

papers.title: Redox regulation of 2-carboxy-D-arabinitol 1-phosphate phosphatase in Fabaceae is associated with high Rubisco dark inhibition
papers.abstract: Improving Rubisco regulation is an avenue for improving crop output. Minimizing the buildup of Rubisco inhibitors can allow improved catalytic activity and CO2 assimilation. The enzyme 2-carboxy-D-arabinitol 1-phosphate phosphatase (CA1Pase) degrades certain Rubisco inhibitors, yet the mechanisms for its regulation, including the function of its C domain, are not well understood. In this study we analysed Vigna unguiculata (cowpea) CA1Pase in silico and in vitro for structural regions and motifs related to regulation of phosphatase activity. We identified a highly conserved cysteine pair motif tied to redox regulation and potential homodimer formation. Variations in one or both cysteine residues in this motif across species correlate with lower dark inhibitor accumulation levels as compared to related species. The C domain is identified as having a regulatory function and potential evolutionary origins are explored. These insights may inform future efforts toward optimising Rubisco's complex regulatory processes including inhibitor degradation.

papers.title: Higher stomatal density and smaller stomatal size associate with higher grain yield in winter wheat
papers.abstract: In wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), flag leaf is crucial in determining grain-filling rate and final grain yield. Stomata, microscopic pores on plant surfaces, balance CO2 uptake and evaporative water loss; their numbers and aperture sizes depend on environmental factors. Previous studies have reported associations between stomatal traits and grain yield; mostly under controlled conditions. Our study aimed to investigate flag leaf stomatal anatomical and physiological traits, and their relationships with winter wheat grain yield under field conditions. We measured stomatal density and size, and stomatal conductance on adaxial and abaxial flag leaf surfaces in a three-year field study with twenty-five winter wheat varieties. Stomatal density ratio remained constant despite different stomatal densities occurring in different years, indicating coordinated adjustments of stomatal numbers between leaf surfaces in response to environmental conditions. Stomatal conductance ratios varied widely, indicating leaf-surface specific stomatal responses to environmental conditions. Grain yield was positively associated with stomatal density and negatively with stomatal size. Flag leaf removal reduced grain weight per spike and did not affect grain numbers per spike, unlike in spring wheat. Our field study provides valuable insights into the relationships between winter wheat stomatal traits and grain yield that can be used in breeding.

papers.title: Genomic signatures of local adaptation in marram grass highlight the importance of provenance in dune restoration
papers.abstract: Coastal sand dunes provide critical natural flood defences and key habitats for a range of threatened species. These systems are formed when shifting sands are stabilised by specialised coastal grasses. In Europe, marram grass (Calamagrostis arenaria) is the main dune building species. However, despite its ecological importance and its widespread use in dune restoration, little is known about the genomic innovations that facilitated the colonisation of the coast, the extent of local adaptation in current populations, or the genetic consequences of restoration practices. Using a chromosome-scale reference genome we generate here, we show that C. arenaria has significant expansions in several gene families relevant to coastal adaptation, including those associated with salinity, drought, and nutrient limitation. Using ddRAD-Seq data for over 200 individuals from 10 European populations, we identified strong genetic differentiation between northern and southern populations which corresponds to recognised subspecies. Within the northern european populations, the genetic structure is largely driven by isolation-by-distance. Although, we detected evidence of non-local planting in a restored Swedish dune system, where introduced plants were genetically distinct from the native population and both groups exhibited reduced genetic diversity. Genome-wide scans for local adaptation within the northern European marram grass individuals identified outlying genomic regions that were enriched for genes with functions associated with nutrient deficiency, drought, pathogen defence, and other environmental stressors characteristic of coastal dunes, potentially indicating local adaptation. Outlying regions also include genes associated with lignin biosynthesis and culm mechanical strength, potentially reflecting selection on the structural properties required to withstand different burial and wind exposure regimes. Overall, these findings show widespread local adaptation in C. arenaria, and support the use of local provenance in dune restoration and conservation.

papers.title: Genome-scale modelling and stable isotope tracing reveal dynamic metabolic reprogramming in a human cardiac hypertrophy model
papers.abstract: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is associated with metabolic remodelling; however the temporal dynamics of this remodelling remain poorly defined in human cardiomyocyte systems. Here, we combined transcriptomic profiling, genome-scale metabolic modelling and stable isotope-resolved metabolomics (SIRM) to map the metabolic consequences of endothelin-1 (ET-1) stimulation in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs). Integration of RNA sequencing data obtained after 8 and 48 hours of ET-1 treatment with the Human2.0 genome-scale metabolic model predicted time-dependent remodelling, characterised by progressive increases in glycolytic flux, enhanced glucose carbon entry into the TCA cycle, and a decrease in fatty acid {beta}-oxidation. Computational flux predictions were independently confirmed by extracellular flux analysis and 13C-substrate tracing, with concordance between modelled and measured fluxes. Extracellular flux analysis showed increased glycolytic capacity and mitochondrial respiration after 48 hours, with greater sensitivity to inhibition of mitochondrial pyruvate transport. Glucose tracing revealed increased 13C enrichment of glycolytic, pentose phosphate pathway, serine-glycine and TCA cycle metabolites, consistent with altered glucose-derived carbon allocation. Increased m+3 labelling of selected TCA-related metabolites was compatible with pyruvate anaplerosis, although pathway-specific fluxes were not resolved. In three-dimensional engineered heart tissue (EHTs) treated with ET-1 for 7 days, increased hypertrophic marker expression was accompanied by a blunted inotropic response, and metabolomics showed similar changes in metabolite abundance and glucose-derived labelling to 2D cultures. These findings support hiPSC-CMs and EHTs as complementary platforms for studying early metabolic remodelling in pathological cardiac hypertrophy and provide an integrated framework linking model predictions to functional and isotope-tracing measurements.

papers.title: SAMP1/TMEM201 protects alveolar type 2 cells from DNA damage-associated senescence and restrains pulmonary fibrosis
papers.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive interstitial lung disease in which repetitive injury to the alveolar epithelium and senescence of alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells drive persistent myofibroblast activation and extracellular matrix deposition. Inner nuclear membrane (INM) proteins organise nuclear architecture and participate in the DNA damage response, but whether they influence epithelial senescence and fibrogenesis is unknown. Here we identify SAMP1/TMEM201, an INM protein that binds lamin A/C, emerin and LINC-complex components, as a compartment-selective protector of AT2 cells. In the bleomycin model of pulmonary fibrosis, SAMP1 was reduced in AT2 cells but unchanged in lung fibroblasts. AT2 cell-specific deletion of Samp1 (Sftpc-Cre^ERT2^; Samp1^flox/flox^) aggravated fibrosis at day 21, with higher Ashcroft scores and increased pulmonary Tnfa and Acta2 expression, whereas intratracheal delivery of AAV6-CAG-Samp1 before bleomycin attenuated both histological fibrosis and these transcriptional responses. In primary AT2 cells analysed immediately after isolation without in vitro stimulation, SAMP1 loss was accompanied by reduced 53BP1 protein, comparable gammaH2AX levels, and upregulation of the senescence-associated and profibrotic markers p16^INK4a^ and PAI-1. These findings define a SAMP1-AT2 senescence axis that constrains pulmonary fibrogenesis and suggest that preserving INM-dependent genome surveillance in the alveolar epithelium may offer an epithelium-directed therapeutic strategy for IPF. Because DNA damage signalling was assessed only under baseline conditions, the data establish an association with altered DNA damage signalling rather than a definitive defect in lesion repair.

papers.title: Integrating Microbial Ecology and Sustainability: Linking Agricultural Waste Gas Streams to Microbial Community Shifts in a Photobioreactor
papers.abstract: Photobioreactors (PBRs) coupled to animal housing offer potential for mitigating gaseous emissions such as CO2 and NH3 while simultaneously producing biomass. Here, we present a time-resolved characterization of microbial community dynamics, with a focus on the genetic potential for carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Using a cone-shaped, helical PBR cultivating Arthrospira platensis (Spirulina) and supplied with exhaust air from a chicken house, we characterized microbial communities over continuous exhaust-air exposure and periodic biomass harvesting. Microbiome and gene-centric profiling revealed temporal variation in community composition and in the representation of genes associated with carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Cycle-based dissolved inorganic nitrogen balances showed that the decrease in dissolved inorganic nitrogen was only partially recovered in harvested biomass, while ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms were associated with structured, low-light niches. These observations indicate ammonia-oxidizing potential but do not establish a quantitatively relevant nitrification flux. Structured carrier matrices provided attached-growth niches harboring microbial populations underrepresented in the circulating suspension, while pre-colonized carriers facilitated biomass development during re-inoculation. Overall, our results show that coupling PBRs to agricultural exhaust streams can support biomass production while sustaining spatially structured microbial communities with taxonomic and functional potential. These findings may inform their further development for emission mitigation and circular biomass production.

papers.title: Structural determinants underlie the essentiality of the m-type thioredoxin TrxA in Synechocystis
papers.abstract: Thioredoxins are central regulators of thiol-based redox signaling in photosynthetic organisms, where multiple isoforms with partially overlapping functions coexist. Among them, TrxA is the cyanobacterial homolog of chloroplast m-type thioredoxins and the only thioredoxin known to be essential in cyanobacteria. However, it is unclear whether this essentiality is due to its high intracellular abundance or to its specific molecular properties. Here, we evaluated the ability of different thioredoxins to functionally replace TrxA and used TrxA/TrxB chimeras to identify the structural determinants underlying its functional specificity. Overexpression of TrxB, TrxQ or TrxC did not support complete segregation of a disrupted trxA locus, although the proteins accumulated to levels comparable to those of endogenous TrxA. Similarly, heterologous expression of NTRC did not rescue the phenotype associated with reduced TrxA levels. Comparative structural analysis revealed differences in surface electrostatics and structural features surrounding the catalytic site of TrxA compared with the other thioredoxins. Analysis of TrxB/TrxA chimeras showed that determinants required for functional complementation are primarily located within the C-terminal region of TrxA. Chimeric variants also differed in their ability to activate cyanobacterial FBP/SBPase and pea chloroplast FBPase in vitro, supporting a role for this region in target-specific interactions. Together, these results demonstrate that the essential function of TrxA cannot be explained by protein abundance alone and requires molecular determinants located primarily within its C-terminal region.

papers.title: Thermosensory pathway makes a U-turn to respond to heat
papers.abstract: Plant organs exhibit a unimodal growth response to temperature, yet the mechanistic links connecting growth-promoting and growth-inhibiting thermal ranges remain unresolved. In Arabidopsis seedlings, warm temperatures promote hypocotyl elongation by relieving phytochrome B (phyB) inhibition, thereby activating the transcription factors PIF4 and PIF7 to drive auxin synthesis. Here, we demonstrate that temperatures beyond the growth optimum actively suppress growth by downregulating auxin levels, auxin signalling, and PIF4 abundance specifically within the cotyledons, the primary site of auxin production. Strikingly, whereas warm temperatures induce the shrinking of phyB nuclear bodies, heat stress causes phyB to assemble into enlarged condensates, a behaviour faithfully recapitulated in mammalian cells, demonstrating an intrinsic biophysical mechanism. Together, our findings indicate that heat-induced growth inhibition is not merely passive stress damage, but an active molecular reversal of the promotive pathway of thermomorphogenesis.

papers.title: HomoeoGWAS enables experiment-wide homoeolog-group interaction mapping in allopolyploid crops
papers.abstract: Allopolyploid crops carry homoeologous gene copies from divergent subgenomes, an evolutionarily defined set of candidate interactions that association studies do not test directly. HomoeoGWAS uses these copies to define the unit of interaction testing, the homoeolog group, and analyses all eligible groups as one family with experiment-wide error calibration, combining three complementary genotype encodings per edge with a structure-aware parametric bootstrap. Family-wise error was controlled in 80-group tests in wheat, cotton and rapeseed under several null models and in full-family tests of all four crops under a structure-aligned global null (379-17,404 groups). The omnibus outperformed a SNP-by-SNP scan when interaction spanned several genotype dimensions. HomoeoGWAS detected homoeolog-group interactions for heading date in wheat, flowering time in rapeseed and fibre length in cotton; five groups at four loci retained support after regional conditioning. Rapeseed homoeolog coupling showed a weak but reproducible association with homoeologous-exchange frequency. Genome-wide interaction analyses took minutes.

papers.title: SEC16A/MAG5-mediated ER export shapes ABA receptor homeostasis
papers.abstract: The phytohormone abscisic acid (ABA) controls plant adaptation to environmental stress through PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors. Regulated receptor turnover through ubiquitination and endosomal trafficking, including ESCRT-dependent vacuolar degradation, is a major mechanism controlling ABA signalling. However, whether ABA receptor homeostasis is established during the early secretory pathway remains unknown. Using complementary cell biological and biochemical approaches, we define a constitutive early secretory pool of the ABA receptors PYR1 and PYL4 associated with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and the Golgi apparatus (GA). Genetic, cell biological and pharmacological analyses reveal that the COPII scaffold protein SEC16A (also known as MAG5) is required for the proper trafficking and homeostasis of this receptor pool. Loss of MAG5 causes intracellular receptor accumulation, impaired trafficking towards late endosomal compartments and enhanced ABA signalling without affecting endogenous ABA accumulation. Together, our findings establish the early secretory pathway as an integral component of the ABA signalling network and demonstrate that MAG5-mediated ER export shapes ABA receptor homeostasis by coordinating receptor trafficking throughout the endomembrane system, revealing the ER as a key regulatory compartment for ABA receptor homeostasis.
